title: Kinzua Bridge State Park, Mt. Jewett, Pennsylvania
seoTitle: Charter Bus to Kinzua Bridge State Park, Pennsylvania
excerpt: A charter bus to Kinzua Bridge State Park brings a group to the Sky Walk and its glass floor. What to expect, vehicle sizing, and how to plan the drive.

heroImage.alt: The Kinzua Sky Walk extending out over the gorge on the remaining piers of the old viaduct

extraImage.alt: Collapsed steel towers of the Kinzua Viaduct lying in the valley below the Sky Walk

body.text: The Kinzua Viaduct was finished in 1882 and was, briefly, the tallest railroad bridge in the world at 301 feet. In 2003 a tornado tore through the valley and dropped eleven of its towers. Pennsylvania decided not to rebuild it, and instead turned the surviving half into a walkway that ends in a glass floor above the wreckage. A charter bus to Kinzua Bridge State Park is the practical way to reach it, because it sits a long way from anywhere in the northern Alleghenies.
What the visit involves

The Sky Walk runs about 600 feet out along the remaining piers, ending at an observation deck with a partial glass floor looking straight down to the twisted towers lying where they fell. It is level, paved and fully accessible, which makes this an unusually easy destination for a mixed-ability group — nobody is excluded from the main attraction.

The visitor center at the entrance covers the bridge's construction and the tornado, and there is a short film. Below the rim, the Kinzua Creek Trail switchbacks down into the gorge for anybody who wants to stand among the fallen steel, which is a steep mile and a genuinely different experience from looking at it from above.
Admission is free. Allow two hours for the Sky Walk and visitor center, or three and a half if part of the group is going down into the gorge.
Which charter bus suits the trip

items: Forty to fifty-six: a full-size [charter bus](/fleet/charter-buses) is comfortable for what is a long drive from almost any direction, and the park has parking that takes coaches.
Twenty to thirty-two: a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) suits a senior travel club or a smaller society outing and handles the rural approach easily.
Ten to fourteen: a [sprinter van](/fleet/sprinter-vans) works for a small photography or railway-history group.

body.text: The on-board restroom is worth having. This corner of Pennsylvania has long gaps between services, and the approach from the south crosses the Allegheny National Forest with very little in it.
Getting there

The park is near Mt. Jewett in McKean County. From [Bradford](/locations/pennsylvania/bradford) it is about half an hour, from [Kane](/locations/pennsylvania/kane) around twenty minutes, and from [Erie](/locations/pennsylvania/erie) roughly two hours. Pittsburgh is a little over three hours and Buffalo about two, which is why groups often pair it with the Allegheny National Forest rather than treating it as a stop on its own.

Anyone searching for charter bus rental near me for northern Pennsylvania should be realistic about the distances. This is a strong half-day destination inside a full-day trip, and the drive is a substantial part of what you are booking.
Making a full day of it

Kinzua is a strong two hours and a long way from anywhere, so pairing it is not optional for most groups — it is what turns a lot of driving into a proper trip. The Allegheny National Forest surrounds the park, and the Kinzua Dam and Allegheny Reservoir sit about an hour west with overlooks that take a coach.

For railway groups, the Knox and Kane railroad history that built the viaduct runs through the whole region, and the small town of Kane makes an easy lunch stop twenty minutes away. Bradford, half an hour north, has the Zippo Case Museum, which is a more entertaining hour than it sounds and works well for a mixed group.

If your group is coming from Pittsburgh or Buffalo, consider an overnight rather than a day trip. Three hours each way for a two-hour attraction is a hard sell, and the region has enough in it to justify staying — particularly in October, when the drive itself becomes part of the reason to come.
When to go

items: October: peak autumn color across the gorge, and comfortably the best time to see it. Book early, because everybody else knows this too.
May to September: warm, green and quiet on weekdays. The gorge trail is at its most pleasant.
Winter: the Sky Walk stays open but the deck can ice and the wind across the gorge is severe. The visitor center keeps shorter hours.

body.text: The glass floor, and who will not use it

The observation deck at the end of the Sky Walk has a partial glass floor looking straight down about 225 feet to the valley. It is entirely safe and a reliable proportion of any group will not stand on it, which is worth mentioning cheerfully in advance rather than discovering as a standoff at the end of the walkway.

There is plenty of solid deck around it, so nobody has to. The view of the collapsed towers below is just as good from the railing, and the fallen steel is more legible from there than from directly above it.

The other thing groups underestimate is wind. The Sky Walk is fully exposed at the top of a gorge, and it is consistently colder and windier out on the deck than it is in the car park. Bring a layer even on a warm day, particularly for a senior group who will otherwise turn back before reaching the end.
